spans.assertion: the analysis examined whether referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned than light-skinned players, using 146,028 player-referee dyads (2,053 players, 3,147 referees) from the 2012-2013 season in England, Germany, France and Spain
after adjustment, dark-skinned players had a 0.168 percentage point higher probability of a red card than light-skinned players (95% CI -0.019 to 0.356, p=0.078)
the hypothesis is not supported because the adjusted result is not statistically significant at α=0.05 using player-level clustered standard errors and the CI includes zero
the primary estimand is the adjusted percentage-point change in P(red card) comparing dark-skinned (≥0.5) to light-skinned (<0.5) players
the adjusted risk difference was found to be 0.168 percentage points (95% CI -0.019 to 0.356; p=0.078)
the RD represents ~14% relative increase over the 1.23% baseline rate, but the CI includes zero so the null cannot be ruled out at 95% confidence
the adjusted odds ratio was found to be 1.149 (95% CI 0.984 to 1.341; p=0.078)
the odds of a red card are 14.9% higher for dark-skinned players, with a CI that marginally includes the null value of 1.0

spans.note: Section 3 heading: Model and Estimation Details.

spans.assertion: the unit of analysis is the player-referee dyad, representing encounters and outcomes between a player and a referee
the total dataset contains 146,028 dyads
all 146,028 dyads (100%) have skin tone ratings
115,457 dyads (79.1%) were complete cases used for analysis
30,571 dyads (20.9%) were excluded for missing covariates, primarily missing player position (12.1%), weight (1.5%), and height/referee bias (<1%)
the analysis sample includes 1,419 unique players
the analysis sample includes 2,893 unique referees
there were 1,455 red card events, 1.26% of dyads
skin tone was measured as the average of two independent raters' assessments of player photos on a 5-point scale
inter-rater reliability was found to be Pearson r=0.923 with 76.8% exact agreement
dark skin was defined as an average rating ≥0.5 and light skin as <0.5
in the analysis sample, 22.9% of players were categorized dark-skinned and 77.1% light-skinned
the outcome was defined as a binary indicator for receiving at least one red card (direct or second-yellow) across all dyad encounters
the model adjusted for standardized number of games in the dyad
the model adjusted for player position across 12 categories
the model adjusted for league country across 4 categories
the model adjusted for standardized player height
the model adjusted for standardized player weight
the model adjusted for standardized referee country implicit bias (meanIAT)
the model adjusted for standardized referee country explicit bias (meanExp)
logistic regression was used as the model
maximum likelihood was used for estimation
standard errors were clustered at the player level to account for non-independence of multiple dyads per player
the risk difference was calculated using average marginal effects via the delta method
the analysis was run in Python 3.11 using statsmodels 0.14.0
the model's McFadden pseudo R² was found to be 0.073
the model converged successfully in 9 iterations
the model had 21 parameters
the crude red card rate for light-skinned players was 1.23% (1,097/89,019 dyads)
the crude red card rate for dark-skinned players was 1.35% (358/26,438 dyads)
the unadjusted risk difference was 0.122 percentage points (95% CI -0.063 to 0.301, p>0.05)
the unadjusted relative risk was 1.099
the adjusted RD being larger than the unadjusted RD suggests confounders partially masked the association, though both estimates are non-significant with player-level clustering
very dark skin (≥0.75) was compared to very light skin (≤0.25), excluding intermediate ratings
the extremes-comparison subsample had N=99,535 dyads
the adjusted RD for extremes was found to be 0.212 percentage points (95% CI -0.019 to 0.444)
the extremes-comparison p-value was 0.072
the adjusted OR for extremes was found to be 1.194 (95% CI 0.984 to 1.448)
the larger effect at extremes (0.212 vs 0.168pp) suggests a potential dose-response relationship, though still non-significant

spans.note: Sensitivity Analysis 2 subheading: Continuous Skin Tone.

spans.assertion: skin tone was modeled as a continuous variable, per 0.25-unit increase
the adjusted RD per 0.25-unit increase was found to be 0.071 percentage points (95% CI 0.012 to 0.129)
this result used robust HC1 standard errors and had p=0.018
the adjusted OR per 0.25-unit increase was found to be 1.060 (95% CI 1.010 to 1.112)
the continuous-model result is interpreted as statistically significant evidence of a graded dose-response relationship rather than a threshold effect
the primary model was re-estimated using referee-level clustering instead of player-level clustering
with referee-level clustering, the adjusted RD was found to be 0.168 percentage points (95% CI 0.016 to 0.321)
with referee-level clustering, p=0.031
with referee-level clustering, the adjusted OR was found to be 1.149, with the same CI as the primary model

referee-level clustering makes the result statistically significant, showing inference is sensitive to the clustering choice; player-level clustering is treated as the more conservative and appropriate choice since skin tone is a player-level characteristic
the analysis tested whether referee country implicit bias moderates the skin tone–red card association
the interaction coefficient was found to be -0.0425 (SE 0.0499)
the interaction p-value was 0.391
no evidence was found that referee country implicit bias moderates the skin tone effect

spans.note: Section 6 heading: Key Covariates and Confounding.
Subheading introducing the 'number of games' covariate discussion.

spans.assertion: the games covariate coefficient was found to be 0.470 (SE 0.015), p<0.001
each SD increase in games played is associated with a 60% increase in the odds of a red card (OR=1.60)
more games played is justified as providing more opportunities for red-card-relevant incidents

spans.note: Caveat that variation in photo standardization/angle/lighting could introduce measurement error in skin tone ratings.
Caveat that the binary 0.5-threshold categorization may obscure graded effects.
Caveat that random (non-differential) misclassification would bias estimates toward the null, potentially explaining the non-significant result.
Caveat that dyads have a complex crossed dependence structure that standard logistic regression assumes away.

spans.assertion: two-way clustering would have been the ideal approach but was not used because it is computationally intensive at this sample size

spans.note: Caveat that within-player correlation may violate independence assumptions; clustering adjusts SEs but not point estimates.
Subheading: Ecological Fallacy for Referee Bias.

spans.assertion: implicit and explicit bias were measured at the referee country level rather than the individual referee level

spans.note: Caveat that country-level associations may not reflect individual-level processes (ecological bias).
Caveat that the analysis cannot determine whether individual referees' attitudes drive the association.

spans.assertion: three sensitivity analyses were conducted without a formal correction for multiple comparisons

spans.note: Caveat that treating the tests as a family would inflate Type I error risk.
Argument that the sensitivity analyses are exploratory/confirmatory rather than separate hypothesis tests.
Restates that data come from the 2012-2013 season in four European leagues only.
Caveat that results may not generalize to other periods, regions, or divisions.
Caveat that the player pool is limited to male first-division players and cannot generalize to women's soccer or lower divisions.

spans.assertion: red cards were aggregated to the dyad level, counting any red card across all games in the dyad
the outcome does not distinguish the frequency (1 vs 2 red cards) or context (direct vs second yellow) of red cards

spans.note: Caveat that the binary outcome may lose information about within-dyad variation.
Caveat that some player-position/league combinations have very few observations, potentially violating positivity.
Caveat that the model extrapolates to sparse covariate combinations, which may be unreliable.

spans.assertion: one possible interpretation is that there is truly no association between skin tone and red card probability once confounders are adjusted
another possibility is a true effect too small to detect reliably; post-hoc power was found to be ~60% to detect a 0.15pp difference
another possibility is that the effect varies by subgroup in ways not captured by the main model, though interaction tests did not reveal significant moderation and power for interactions is low
another possibility is that non-differential measurement error in skin tone attenuated the true effect toward zero
another possibility is that publication bias and prior use of this public dataset influenced variable selection and model specification, potentially introducing bias

spans.note: Section 10 heading: Recommendations for Future Research.
Recommends larger, multi-season/multi-league samples for future research.
Recommends collecting individual-level referee bias measures in future research.
Recommends including in-game context variables in future research.
Recommends objective colorimetry-based skin tone measurement in future research.
Recommends event-level rather than dyad-level analysis in future research.
Recommends a randomized audit study using video vignettes.
Recommends mixed-effects/crossed random-effects models in future research.
Recommends pre-registering the analysis plan in future research.
Transition sentence noting several findings warrant consideration despite non-significance.

spans.assertion: all point estimates (primary, both sensitivity analyses, unadjusted) favor the hypothesized direction, providing some non-conclusive weight of evidence
the significant continuous-skin-tone result (p=0.018) is interpreted as supporting a gradual, graded increase in red card risk with darker skin tone
the 0.17pp effect is interpreted as roughly 1 additional red card per 588 dyads, which at the population level could mean dozens of additional red cards attributable to skin tone

spans.note: General statement that even small officiating biases matter given the stakes of professional soccer.
Cites Silberzahn et al. 2018 as having found similarly small, marginally significant effects depending on analytic approach.
Transition sentence introducing the final assessment bullets.

spans.assertion: the point estimate of 0.168pp (14% relative increase) suggests a small but non-trivial disparity
the 95% CI (-0.019, 0.356) includes zero, indicating insufficient evidence to rule out no effect
the p-value of 0.078 marginally exceeds the α=0.05 threshold, failing conventional significance
the direction of the effect is consistently positive across all analyses

the overall verdict is that the hypothesis is not supported; evidence is inconclusive given the uncertainty and lack of significance under player-level clustering, though a small effect cannot be definitively ruled out, and further research is recommended
